questions.source_name: Current Electricity Worksheet · L1-Q01 · APPLY · D2 (proposed)
questions.subtopic: Electric Charge, Current and Potential Difference
questions.stem: A steady current of 3.2 A flows through a wire for 10 s. The number of electrons crossing a cross-section of the wire in this time is (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C):

hints.text: What is current per second?
Use Q=It and Q=Ne.
Relate the number to total charge.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: I=3.2 A, t=10 s.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: Q=It=32 C.
3. Execution & Resolution: N=32/(1.6×10⁻¹⁹)=2×10²⁰.
questions.check: Multiplying N by e gives 32 C.

questions.source_name: Current Electricity Worksheet · L1-Q02 · APPLY · D2 (proposed)
questions.subtopic: Electric Charge, Current and Potential Difference
questions.stem: A device has a potential difference of 6 V across it. A total charge of 600 C passes through it in 2 minutes. The power consumed by the device is:

hints.text: Convert minutes to seconds.
Use I=Q/t and P=VI.
Calculate current before power.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Q=600 C, t=120 s, V=6 V.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: I=600/120=5 A.
3. Execution & Resolution: P=6×5=30 W.
questions.check: VQ=3600 J, equal to Pt.

questions.source_name: Current Electricity Worksheet · L1-Q03 · REPRESENT · D2 (proposed)
questions.subtopic: Electric Charge, Current and Potential Difference
questions.stem:
The current through a wire varies with time as shown in Fig. 1. The total charge that flows through the wire in 15 s is:
[FIG-stem-1]

hints.text: What does area under I–t represent?
Split the graph into geometric shapes.
Use the two triangles and rectangle.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Vertices (0,0), (5,4), (10,4), (15,0).
2. Physical Model & Formulation: Charge is the area under current versus time.
3. Execution & Resolution: Q=½(5)(4)+5(4)+½(5)(4)=40 C.
questions.check: Mean current 40/15 A is less than peak 4 A.

questions.source_name: Current Electricity Worksheet · L1-Q04 · EXPLAIN · D2 (proposed)
questions.subtopic: Electric Charge, Current and Potential Difference
questions.stem: Which of the following statements about conduction in a metallic wire carrying a steady current is/are correct? [One or more options may be correct.]
options: A: The drift speed of the free electrons is very small, of the order of mm/s.
B: The electric field that drives the current is set up in the wire almost at the speed of light.
C: The number of electrons crossing every cross-section per second is the same, even if the wire has non-uniform thickness.
D: Each free electron moves along the wire at constant speed without collisions.
questions.answer: A, B, C: The drift speed of the free electrons is very small, of the order of mm/s.; The electric field that drives the current is set up in the wire almost at the speed of light.; The number of electrons crossing every cross-section per second is the same, even if the wire has non-uniform thickness.

hints.text: Separate drift and signal propagation.
Apply steady-state charge continuity.
Evaluate the claims about collisions and cross-section.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Metallic conduction has mean drift and random scattering.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: The field propagates rapidly, and steady current is conserved across sections.
3. Execution & Resolution: A, B, C are correct; D is false because electrons scatter.
questions.check: Signal speed depends on the circuit environment; it is distinct from drift speed.

questions.source_name: Current Electricity Worksheet · L1-Q05 · APPLY · D2 (proposed)
questions.subtopic: Electric Charge, Current and Potential Difference
questions.stem: A steady current flows through a wire whose thicker part has three times the cross-sectional area of its thinner part. The ratio of the drift speed of electrons in the thinner part to that in the thicker part is:

hints.text: What quantity is constant along a steady wire?
For the same material I=neAv_d.
Compare drift speeds at fixed current.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Areas are A and 3A, with equal carrier density.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: v_d=I/(neA).
3. Execution & Resolution: v_thin/v_thick=3A/A=3:1.
questions.check: The thinner section has greater drift speed.

questions.source_name: Current Electricity Worksheet · L1-Q06 · APPLY · D2 (proposed)
questions.subtopic: Electric Charge, Current and Potential Difference
questions.stem: At a junction in a circuit, currents of 5 A and 3 A flow into the junction. Two wires carry 2 A and 4 A away from the junction. A fifth wire is also connected to the junction. The current in it is:
options: A: 2 A, flowing towards the junction
B: 6 A, flowing away from the junction
C: 2 A, flowing away from the junction
D: 6 A, flowing towards the junction
questions.answer: C: 2 A, flowing away from the junction

hints.text: Separate incoming and outgoing arrows.
Use conservation of charge at a junction.
Find the signed difference of known currents.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: In: 5+3 A. Known out: 2+4 A.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: Kirchhoff current law: sum in=sum out.
3. Execution & Resolution: 8−6=2 A must flow away.
questions.check: 8 A in equals 8 A out.

questions.source_name: Current Electricity Worksheet · L1-Q07 · MODEL · D2 (proposed)
questions.subtopic: Ohm's Law, Resistance and Resistivity
questions.stem: The resistance of a wire is 10 Ω. It is uniformly stretched to twice its original length (its volume remains the same). The new resistance is:

hints.text: What changes when length doubles at fixed volume?
Use R=ρL/A, with fixed resistivity.
Express the new length and area as ratios.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: R=10 Ω; L′=2L, A′=A/2.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: R′/R=(L′/L)(A/A′)=4.
3. Execution & Resolution: R′=40 Ω.
questions.check: Both geometric changes increase resistance.

questions.source_name: Current Electricity Worksheet · L1-Q08 · APPLY · D2 (proposed)
questions.subtopic: Ohm's Law, Resistance and Resistivity
questions.stem: A wire of resistance 64 Ω is cut into four equal pieces, and the four pieces are connected in parallel. The equivalent resistance is:

hints.text: First find resistance of one piece.
Identical parallel paths add conductances.
Find the equivalent of four equal pieces.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Each of four pieces has 64/4=16 Ω.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: R_eq=R_piece/4.
3. Execution & Resolution: R_eq=4 Ω.
questions.check: The equivalent is below 16 Ω.

questions.source_name: Current Electricity Worksheet · L1-Q09 · APPLY · D2 (proposed)
questions.subtopic: Ohm's Law, Resistance and Resistivity
questions.stem: Two wires of the same material have lengths in the ratio 1 : 2 and radii in the ratio 1 : 2. The ratio of their resistances is:

hints.text: Relate radius to area.
Use R=ρL/(πr²).
Form the ratio before substitution.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: L₁/L₂=1/2, r₁/r₂=1/2.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: R₁/R₂=(L₁/L₂)(r₂/r₁)².
3. Execution & Resolution: R₁/R₂=2:1.
questions.check: Doubling radius quadruples area.

questions.source_name: Current Electricity Worksheet · L1-Q10 · REPRESENT · D2 (proposed)
questions.subtopic: Ohm's Law, Resistance and Resistivity
questions.stem:
Fig. 2 shows the V–I graphs for two ohmic conductors A and B. The ratio of their resistances R_A : R_B is:
[FIG-stem-1]
questions.figure_note: Fig. 2: V–I graphs of two conductors

hints.text: Read both voltages at one current.
Resistance is slope on a V–I plot for an ohmic wire.
Compare the slopes.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: At 2 A, A has 4 V and B has 8 V.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: R_A=2 Ω, R_B=4 Ω.
3. Execution & Resolution: R_A:R_B=1:2.
questions.check: The steeper line has greater resistance.

questions.source_name: Current Electricity Worksheet · L1-Q11 · EXPLAIN · D2 (proposed)
questions.subtopic: Ohm's Law, Resistance and Resistivity
questions.stem:
Fig. 3 shows the V–I graph of a filament lamp. Which of the following statements is/are correct? [One or more options may be correct.]
[FIG-stem-1]
options: A: The increase in resistance is due to the rise in temperature of the filament.
B: The resistance of the filament increases as the current increases.
C: The lamp obeys Ohm's law over the whole range of current.
D: At every point the resistance of the lamp equals the slope of the graph at that point.
questions.answer: A, B: The increase in resistance is due to the rise in temperature of the filament.; The resistance of the filament increases as the current increases.
questions.figure_note: Fig. 3: V–I graph of a filament lamp

hints.text: Is the graph a straight line?
Static resistance V/I differs from tangent slope.
Evaluate heating, resistance and Ohm's law separately.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: The filament graph curves upward as the filament heats.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: V/I increases; tangent slope is differential resistance.
3. Execution & Resolution: A and B are correct; C and D are false.
questions.check: Only a linear graph through the origin has constant V/I and equal differential resistance.

questions.source_name: Current Electricity Worksheet · L1-Q12 · EXPLAIN · D2 (proposed)
questions.subtopic: Ohm's Law, Resistance and Resistivity
questions.stem: Which of the following statements is/are correct? [One or more options may be correct.]
options: A: The resistivity of a semiconductor increases when its temperature rises.
B: The resistivity of a metal increases when its temperature rises.
C: Manganin is used for making standard resistors because its resistivity changes very little with temperature.
D: Alloys generally have greater resistivity than the pure metals from which they are made.
questions.answer: B, C, D: The resistivity of a metal increases when its temperature rises.; Manganin is used for making standard resistors because its resistivity changes very little with temperature.; Alloys generally have greater resistivity than the pure metals from which they are made.

hints.text: Distinguish types of materials.
Think about scattering and carrier density.
Evaluate the standard-resistor property separately.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Typical metal resistivity increases with temperature; ordinary semiconductor resistivity decreases.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: Manganin has a small temperature coefficient; alloys generally have greater resistivity.
3. Execution & Resolution: B, C, D are correct in the school-level model; A is false.
questions.check: Temperature behavior depends on material and operating regime.

questions.source_name: Current Electricity Worksheet · L1-Q13 · MODEL · D2 (proposed)
questions.subtopic: Ohm's Law, Resistance and Resistivity
questions.stem:
A uniform wire of total resistance 12 Ω is bent into a circular ring. Two points P and Q on the ring are separated by an arc subtending 120° at the centre, as shown in Fig. 4. The resistance between P and Q is:
[FIG-stem-1]
questions.figure_note: Fig. 4: Uniform wire bent into a ring

hints.text: Identify two arcs between P and Q.
Uniform wire resistance is proportional to length.
Use arc-angle fractions and parallel reduction.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Arcs are 120° and 240° of 12 Ω.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: Their resistances are 4 Ω and 8 Ω.
3. Execution & Resolution: R_eq=4×8/(4+8)=8/3 Ω.
questions.check: Parallel equivalent is less than either arc.

questions.source_name: Current Electricity Worksheet · L1-Q14 · APPLY · D2 (proposed)
questions.subtopic: Ohm's Law, Resistance and Resistivity
questions.stem: When a wire is uniformly stretched so that its length increases by 10% (its volume remaining constant), the percentage increase in its resistance is nearly:

hints.text: Apply the constant-volume constraint.
At fixed resistivity R∝L².
Express new length as a multiple of old length.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: L′=1.1L, A′=A/1.1.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: R′/R=1.1²=1.21.
3. Execution & Resolution: Increase is 21%.
questions.check: The squared factor includes both length and area changes.

questions.source_name: Current Electricity Worksheet · L1-Q15 · APPLY · D2 (proposed)
questions.subtopic: Combination of Resistors
questions.stem: Three resistors of 2 Ω, 3 Ω and 6 Ω are connected in parallel. The equivalent resistance is:

hints.text: Identify the common terminal nodes.
Add conductances.
Use a common denominator for reciprocals.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Parallel resistances 2, 3, 6 Ω.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: 1/R_eq=1/2+1/3+1/6=1 Ω⁻¹.
3. Execution & Resolution: R_eq=1 Ω.
questions.check: Below the smallest branch resistance.

questions.source_name: Current Electricity Worksheet · L1-Q16 · APPLY · D2 (proposed)
questions.subtopic: Combination of Resistors
questions.stem:
In the circuit of Fig. 5, the cell has negligible internal resistance. The current through the 6 Ω resistor is:
[FIG-stem-1]

hints.text: Locate the series and parallel groups.
Find parallel equivalent then total current.
Find voltage across the parallel group.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: 4 Ω in series with 6 Ω∥3 Ω across 12 V.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: R_p=2 Ω; I_total=12/6=2 A; V_p=4 V.
3. Execution & Resolution: I_6=4/6=2/3 A.
questions.check: I_3=4/3 A; branch sum 2 A.

questions.source_name: Current Electricity Worksheet · L1-Q17 · APPLY · D2 (proposed)
questions.subtopic: Combination of Resistors
questions.stem: The ratio of the equivalent resistance of five identical resistors connected in series to that when they are connected in parallel is:

hints.text: Let each resistor be R.
Series adds resistance, parallel adds conductance.
Find the ratio of the equivalents.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Five identical resistors in each arrangement.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: R_series=5R, R_parallel=R/5.
3. Execution & Resolution: Ratio is 25:1.
questions.check: Ratio scales as n².

questions.source_name: Current Electricity Worksheet · L1-Q18 · MODEL · D2 (proposed)
questions.subtopic: Combination of Resistors
questions.stem:
The equivalent resistance between A and B in the network of Fig. 6 is:
[FIG-stem-1]

hints.text: Compare ratios on the two bridge arms.
Equipotential middle nodes carry no bridge current.
Test balance then combine outer paths.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: AC=2, CB=4, AD=3, DB=6, CD=5 Ω.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: 2/4=3/6, hence V_C=V_D.
3. Execution & Resolution: R_eq=6∥9=3.6 Ω.
questions.check: The middle resistor has zero voltage.

questions.source_name: Current Electricity Worksheet · L1-Q19 · SYNTHESIZE · D2 (proposed)
questions.subtopic: Combination of Resistors
questions.stem:
Twelve identical resistors, each of 12 Ω, form the edges of a cube as shown in Fig. 7. The equivalent resistance between the opposite corners A and B of the body diagonal is:
[FIG-stem-1]

hints.text: Group cube vertices by distance from A.
Opposite-terminal symmetry gives equipotential layers.
Count edges between successive layers.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: The layers contain 1,3,3,1 vertices.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: The bundles are 3,6,3 equal resistors in parallel.
3. Execution & Resolution: R_eq=r/3+r/6+r/3=5r/6=10 Ω.
questions.check: Multiple paths lower the resistance below one edge.

questions.source_name: Current Electricity Worksheet · L1-Q20 · APPLY · D2 (proposed)
questions.subtopic: Combination of Resistors
questions.stem: Three resistors, each of resistance R, are connected to form a triangle ABC. The equivalent resistance between the corners A and B is:

hints.text: Trace paths from A to B.
One path goes directly and one via C.
Combine the path resistances in parallel.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Paths have R and 2R.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: 1/R_eq=1/R+1/(2R).
3. Execution & Resolution: R_eq=2R/3.
questions.check: Below R.

questions.source_name: Current Electricity Worksheet · L1-Q21 · MODEL · D2 (proposed)
questions.subtopic: Combination of Resistors
questions.stem:
In the circuit of Fig. 8, the cell has negligible internal resistance. The current through the 2 Ω resistor is:
[FIG-stem-1]

hints.text: Locate the branch with the 2 Ω resistor.
Series elements share current.
Find the branch resistance and voltage.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: 4 Ω and 2 Ω form a branch across 6 V; 3 Ω is another branch.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: The target branch is 6 Ω.
3. Execution & Resolution: I_2=6/6=1 A.
questions.check: Other branch current is 2 A.

questions.source_name: Current Electricity Worksheet · L1-Q22 · MODEL · D2 (proposed)
questions.subtopic: Combination of Resistors
questions.stem:
In the circuit of Fig. 9, the cell has negligible internal resistance. When the switch S is closed (compared with S open), which of the following is/are correct? [One or more options may be correct.]
[FIG-stem-1]
options: A: The power dissipated in the 4 Ω resistor becomes zero.
B: The total power supplied by the cell decreases.
C: The current from the cell increases from 1 A to 3 A.
D: The potential difference across the 2 Ω resistor doubles.
questions.answer: A, C: The power dissipated in the 4 Ω resistor becomes zero.; The current from the cell increases from 1 A to 3 A.
questions.figure_note: Fig. 9: Circuit with a switch across a resistor

hints.text: Draw both switch states.
Closed ideal switch merges endpoint potentials.
Calculate total and individual voltages in each state.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Open: 2+4 Ω across 6 V. Closed: 4 Ω bypassed.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: I_open=1 A, I_closed=3 A; V_2 goes from 2 V to 6 V.
3. Execution & Resolution: A and C correct; B and D false.
questions.check: Cell power rises 6 to 18 W; V_2 triples.

questions.source_name: Current Electricity Worksheet · L1-Q23 · APPLY · D2 (proposed)
questions.subtopic: Heating Effect of Current, Electric Power and Energy
questions.stem: A heater coil of resistance 20 Ω carries a current of 3 A for 5 minutes. The heat produced is:

hints.text: Identify the heating law.
Convert minutes to seconds.
Use I²Rt and convert to kJ.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: I=3 A, R=20 Ω, t=300 s.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: H=I²Rt.
3. Execution & Resolution: H=54000 J=54 kJ.

questions.source_name: Current Electricity Worksheet · L1-Q24 · MODEL · D2 (proposed)
questions.subtopic: Heating Effect of Current, Electric Power and Energy
questions.stem: Two electric bulbs rated 60 W and 100 W, both for 220 V, are connected in series across a 220 V supply. Which statement is correct?
options: A: The 100 W bulb glows brighter than the 60 W bulb
C: Both glow with their rated power
D: The 60 W bulb glows brighter than the 100 W bulb
questions.answer: D: The 60 W bulb glows brighter than the 100 W bulb

hints.text: Compare rated resistances.
At the same rated voltage use R=V²/P, assuming constant rated resistance.
Compare powers with common series current.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Both rated 220 V; idealize filament resistance as fixed.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: R_60>R_100 and P=I²R in series.
3. Execution & Resolution: 60 W bulb dissipates more power and is modeled as brighter (D).
questions.check: Real filament resistance and luminous efficacy vary with temperature; this is an idealized worksheet model.

questions.source_name: Current Electricity Worksheet · L1-Q25 · MODEL · D2 (proposed)
questions.subtopic: Heating Effect of Current, Electric Power and Energy
questions.stem: Two bulbs of 100 W and 25 W, both rated for 220 V, are connected in series across a 220 V supply. The potential difference across the 100 W bulb is:

hints.text: Convert ratings to resistances.
Series voltage divides in proportion to resistance.
Find the 100 W resistance fraction.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: At 220 V, R_100=484 Ω and R_25=1936 Ω, assuming constant rated resistances.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: V_100=220×484/(484+1936).
3. Execution & Resolution: V_100=44 V.
questions.check: The 25 W bulb gets 176 V; actual filament behavior is nonlinear.

questions.source_name: Current Electricity Worksheet · L1-Q26 · APPLY · D2 (proposed)
questions.subtopic: Heating Effect of Current, Electric Power and Energy
questions.stem: Four bulbs of 60 W each are used for 5 hours every day for 30 days. If electrical energy costs ₹ 6 per unit (kWh), the bill for the month is:

hints.text: Convert total power to kW.
Find total operating hours.
Multiply energy by cost per kWh.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Power=0.24 kW; time=150 h.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: Energy=0.24×150=36 kWh.
3. Execution & Resolution: Cost=36×₹6=₹216.
questions.check: Units kW×h×₹/kWh=₹.

questions.source_name: Current Electricity Worksheet · L1-Q27 · APPLY · D2 (proposed)
questions.subtopic: Heating Effect of Current, Electric Power and Energy
questions.stem: An electric heater is rated 2 kW, 220 V. Which of the following fuse ratings is most suitable for its circuit?

hints.text: Find the normal operating current.
Use P=VI.
Choose the smallest listed rating above normal current in the idealized MCQ.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Rated 2000 W, 220 V.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: I=2000/220≈9.09 A.
3. Execution & Resolution: 10 A is the closest listed rating above normal load.
questions.check: Schematic MCQ only; actual protection depends on equipment and applicable regulations.

questions.source_name: Current Electricity Worksheet · L1-Q28 · MODEL · D2 (proposed)
questions.subtopic: Heating Effect of Current, Electric Power and Energy
questions.stem: A heater coil dissipates 1 kW when connected to a mains supply. A piece equal to 1/4 of its length is cut off and the remaining coil is connected to the same supply. The power dissipated is:

hints.text: What fraction of the coil remains?
Resistance scales with length at fixed area and resistivity.
At fixed voltage use P=V²/R.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Remaining length 3/4 of original.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: R′=3R/4, P′/P=R/R′.
3. Execution & Resolution: P′=4/3 kW.

questions.source_name: Current Electricity Worksheet · L1-Q29 · APPLY · D2 (proposed)
questions.subtopic: Heating Effect of Current, Electric Power and Energy
questions.stem: A 1 kW immersion heater has an efficiency of 80%. The time it takes to raise the temperature of 2 kg of water from 20 °C to 70 °C is (specific heat of water = 4200 J kg⁻¹ °C⁻¹):

hints.text: Calculate the temperature rise.
Useful heat is mcΔT; efficiency determines useful power.
Divide required heat by useful power.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: m=2 kg, ΔT=50 °C, c=4200 J kg⁻¹ °C⁻¹.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: Q=420000 J; useful power=800 W.

questions.source_name: Current Electricity Worksheet · L1-Q30 · APPLY · D2 (proposed)
questions.subtopic: Cells, Internal Resistance and Measuring Instruments
questions.stem: A cell of emf 6 V and internal resistance 1 Ω is connected to an external resistance of 5 Ω. The potential difference across the terminals of the cell is:

hints.text: Include the internal resistance.
Use I=E/(R+r).
Find terminal voltage from IR or E−Ir.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: E=6 V, r=1 Ω, R=5 Ω.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: I=6/6=1 A.
3. Execution & Resolution: V_terminal=5 V.

questions.source_name: Current Electricity Worksheet · L1-Q31 · APPLY · D2 (proposed)
questions.subtopic: Cells, Internal Resistance and Measuring Instruments
questions.stem: Three identical cells, each of emf 2 V and internal resistance 0.5 Ω, are connected in series with an external resistor of 4.5 Ω. The current in the resistor is:

hints.text: Assume cells connected in series aiding.
Add emfs and internal resistances.
Use total emf divided by total resistance.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Three cells: E_total=6 V, r_total=1.5 Ω.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: R_total=4.5+1.5=6 Ω.
3. Execution & Resolution: I=1 A.

questions.source_name: Current Electricity Worksheet · L1-Q32 · EXPLAIN · D2 (proposed)
questions.subtopic: Cells, Internal Resistance and Measuring Instruments
questions.stem: Which of the following statements about electrical meters is/are correct? [One or more options may be correct.]
options: A: An ideal voltmeter has infinite resistance.
B: An ideal ammeter has infinite resistance.
C: A voltmeter is connected in parallel across the component whose potential difference is to be measured.
D: An ammeter is connected in series with the part of the circuit whose current is to be measured.
questions.answer: A, C, D: An ideal voltmeter has infinite resistance.; A voltmeter is connected in parallel across the component whose potential difference is to be measured.; An ammeter is connected in series with the part of the circuit whose current is to be measured.

hints.text: What must a meter measure without disturbing the circuit?
Ideal ammeter has zero resistance; ideal voltmeter infinite resistance.
Match each meter to its connection.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Voltmeter measures potential difference; ammeter measures current.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: Voltmeter connects parallel; ammeter series.
3. Execution & Resolution: A,C,D correct; B false.
questions.check: Ideal limits avoid loading and series drop.

questions.source_name: Current Electricity Worksheet · L1-Q33 · MODEL · D2 (proposed)
questions.subtopic: Cells, Internal Resistance and Measuring Instruments
questions.stem:
In the circuit of Fig. 10 the cell has negligible internal resistance and the voltmeter is ideal. The reading of the voltmeter is:
[FIG-stem-1]
questions.figure_note: Fig. 10: Circuit with an ideal voltmeter

Use the series voltage-divider relation.
Find voltage across the 3 Ω resistor.

2. Physical Model & Formulation: I=9/(6+3)=1 A.
3. Execution & Resolution: V_meter=3 V.
questions.check: Voltage drops sum to 9 V.

questions.source_name: Current Electricity Worksheet · L1-Q34 · MODEL · D2 (proposed)
questions.subtopic: Cells, Internal Resistance and Measuring Instruments
questions.stem: A galvanometer of resistance 50 Ω gives full-scale deflection for a current of 5 mA. To convert it into a voltmeter of range 0 to 10 V, a resistance must be connected:

hints.text: Convert full-scale current to amperes.
A voltmeter adds a series resistor.
Find required total resistance, subtract galvanometer resistance.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: G=50 Ω, I_g=0.005 A, V=10 V.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: R_total=V/I_g=2000 Ω.
3. Execution & Resolution: Added series resistance=1950 Ω.
questions.check: At 10 V, current is exactly 5 mA.

questions.source_name: Current Electricity Worksheet · L1-Q35 · REPRESENT · D2 (proposed)
questions.subtopic: Cells, Internal Resistance and Measuring Instruments
questions.stem:
A cell is connected to a variable resistor. The terminal potential difference V of the cell is plotted against the current I drawn from it in Fig. 11. The emf and the internal resistance of the cell are:
[FIG-stem-1]
questions.figure_note: Fig. 11: Terminal potential difference versus current for a cell

hints.text: Read voltage at zero current.
Use V=E−Ir.
Find slope magnitude from a second graph point.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Graph points (0,6) and (2,2).
2. Physical Model & Formulation: E=6 V, r=(6−2)/2.
3. Execution & Resolution: E=6 V, r=2 Ω.
questions.check: Zero-voltage intercept 3 A equals E/r.

questions.stem: A battery of emf 12 V and internal resistance 2 Ω is connected to a 4 Ω resistor and a 12 Ω resistor in parallel. The current through the 12 Ω resistor is:

hints.text: Combine the parallel loads.
Include internal resistance for total current.
Find voltage across the external network then branch current.

steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: 4 Ω∥12 Ω=3 Ω; r=2 Ω.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: I_total=12/5=2.4 A; V_terminal=7.2 V.
3. Execution & Resolution: I_12=7.2/12=0.6 A.
